turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. So, um, I guess I'm here because... well, I work in video production, mostly editing and camera operation, which I've been doing for years, right? Ever since I got my bachelor's. So I should have this all down to an absolute science by now. But it’s just getting to a point where I'm genuinely freaking myself out. My job requires a lot of precision, you know? Like, you have to be on top of a million little moving parts, and I try to be, but... what finally scared me into actually making this appointment and coming in today is that I just keep making these really, really dumb technical mistakes. 

Mistakes I absolutely know better than to make! Like, I’ll be dumping footage and I'll label the camera cards completely wrong, which is a total nightmare for the post-production workflow, let me tell you. It messes everything up down the line. Or I'll be going through a project and I'll just totally miss a specific timecode note from the director. And the worst one recently, the one that really made me pick up the phone to call your office, was when I exported a final cut for a client and sent it off, and it had the completely wrong lower-third graphic on the screen. And the crazy thing is, I swear I checked it! I scrubbed through the timeline, I looked right at it before I hit export, and I still just... missed it. It's so embarrassing and frustrating because I know how to do my job, I'm good at my job, but these stupid little errors just keep happening and I don't know why my brain is doing this.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly describes making careless, detail-oriented mistakes at work, such as mislabeling camera cards, missing timecode notes, and exporting videos with incorrect graphics despite checking them.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed these kinds of mistakes throughout your entire life, even back when you were in school, or is this a relatively new struggle for you?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, gosh, no, it’s definitely not new. I mean, if I really sit and think about it—which I have been doing a lot lately, obviously, since I finally made this appointment—it’s kind of always been a thing. It just... it looks different now that I'm a thirty-eight-year-old adult with a career, you know? But back in school... oh man. 

Even way back in elementary school, I was absolutely *that* kid. My teachers were constantly having to move my desk around the room. Like, I distinctly remember Mrs. Gable in third grade actually dragged my desk right up against her big wooden teacher's desk at the front of the room because I just... I could not stay in my seat. I was always up and wandering around, looking at the class pet or whatever. And the talking! I would constantly be blurting out the answers to questions before she even finished asking them. It wasn't that I was trying to be a bad kid or disrespectful, I just... the thought would pop into my head and it would just fly right out of my mouth before I had a second to filter it. 

And I was always bothering my classmates, too. I'd lean over and start talking to them during quiet reading time, or I'd just start messing with their pencils on their desks, and the crazy part is I honestly wouldn't even realize I was doing it until the teacher snapped at me to turn around and sit still. So, yeah, this whole pattern of just moving too fast and doing things before my brain actually stops to process what's happening... it's really been happening my entire life. I just used to get in trouble for it in a classroom, and now I'm getting in trouble for it with producers and directors.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient states they could not stay in their seat in elementary school and were always up and wandering around.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient mentions 'And the talking!' and describes constantly talking to classmates during quiet times.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly recalls constantly blurting out answers to questions before the teacher finished asking them.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient describes bothering classmates by talking to them and messing with their pencils without realizing it.
